script:
export const meta = {
  name: 'riscv-labs-impl',
  description: 'Implement all six hollowed-out RISC-V CPU labs and verify each by iverilog simulation',
  phases: [
    { title: 'Implement', detail: 'one agent per lab, fills every hole and self-verifies by simulation' },
    { title: 'Verify', detail: 'independent adversarial verification per lab' },
  ],
}

const COMMON = `
# Context

You are working in /workspace/repo — a ZJU Computer Architecture course repo containing SIX
progressive Verilog implementations of an RV32IM CPU (src/lab1 .. src/lab6). Each lab has been
"hollowed out": module bodies were replaced by TODO comments, and some course-skeleton files
still contain \`//fill sth. here\` / \`//need to fill in\` placeholders (which are NOT valid
Verilog and currently break compilation). Your job is to restore a fully working
implementation for ONE lab.

Tooling: Icarus Verilog 12 is installed (\`iverilog\`, \`vvp\`). There is NO Vivado.
Reference documentation for your lab is at /workspace/repo/docs/<lab>.md (Chinese) and
/workspace/repo/src/<lab>/README.md.

# HARD CONSTRAINTS — violating any of these fails the task

1. Only modify files under /workspace/repo/src/<YOUR_LAB>/ . Never touch another lab, never
   touch /workspace/repo/docs, never run git commands (the orchestrator handles commits).
2. Do NOT create new .v / .vh files under /workspace/repo/src/. The hidden grading harness
   compiles a fixed set of files. If you need an extra helper module, define it INSIDE an
   existing .v file of your lab (several modules in one file is legal Verilog).
3. Do NOT rename, remove or reorder existing module names, port names, port order, parameter
   names, or existing internal wire/reg names in the skeleton — most importantly in
   RV32core.v. The hidden tests use hierarchical references into the core (signals such as
   PC_WB, inst_WB, rd_WB, wt_data_WB, RegWrite_WB, wb_addr, wb_data, clk_counter, ALUout_MEM,
   Datain_MEM ...). You MAY add new internal signals and new always/assign blocks.
4. Never define a module whose name might also be supplied by the grader's harness. In
   particular NEVER define or instantiate modules named \`multiplier\`, \`divider\`, or \`RS\`.
   The Vivado IP cores \`multiplier\` and \`divider\` do NOT exist anywhere in this repo, so
   instantiating them would make elaboration fail. Where a TODO says "instantiate multiplier
   IP" / "instantiate divider IP", instead implement the arithmetic with your own helper
   module that has a UNIQUE name (e.g. \`mul_ip_<lab>\`, \`div_ip_<lab>\`) defined at the bottom
   of the same file, preserving the intended latency/handshake behaviour described by the
   surrounding skeleton code.
5. Verilog-2005 compatible code only — \`iverilog -g2005\` must accept it (you may also test
   with -g2012, but do not use SystemVerilog-only constructs such as always_ff, logic,
   typedef, ++, etc.).
6. Keep every \`$readmemh("rom.mem", ...)\` / \`$readmemh("ram.mem", ...)\` string exactly as it
   is. When simulating, either run \`vvp\` from the lab's core/ directory, or copy the .mem
   files next to where you run it.
7. Do not weaken or delete existing correct logic. Do not delete the Chinese comments.

# Method

1. Read EVERY file in your lab directory (core/, common/, auxillary/, sim/, the .s test
   program, README.md) and /workspace/repo/docs/<lab>.md before writing any code.
   Also look at sibling labs for reference implementations of shared blocks: several modules
   (e.g. cmp_32, MUX*, add_32, REG32, ROM_D, debug_clk, and in some labs Regs/ImmGen/RAM_B/
   CtrlUnit) are already implemented in one lab and hollowed in another — copying the working
   sibling version (adapted to the local port list) is encouraged and usually exactly right.
2. Find every hole:  grep -rn "TODO\\|fill sth\\|need to fill" src/<lab>
   (Ignore the single pre-existing board comment \`.btn_c(BTN_C), // TODO\` in auxillary/top.v —
   that is not a hole. Everything else IS a hole and must be filled.)
3. Implement.
4. Build a self-checking testbench under /workspace/agent_tests/<lab>/ (you MAY create files
   there) with a run.sh that compiles + runs it with iverilog and prints a clear PASS/FAIL
   report. Derive the expected results from the lab's own test program and its comments /
   reference material.
5. Iterate until the simulation actually produces the documented architectural behaviour.
   Compiling is NOT enough. Debug with $display/$monitor on the pipeline signals.
6. Re-grep for remaining holes and re-run your test before finishing.

# Final report (plain text, this is your return value)

- List of files changed and a one-line summary of each.
- The exact command to reproduce your test.
- A table: expected vs actual for every checked value, and the overall PASS/FAIL.
- Anything you could not make work, stated honestly.
`;

const LABS = [
  {
    id: 'lab1',
    title: 'Lab 1 — basic 5-stage in-order pipeline',
    prompt: `
# Your lab: src/lab1 — classic 5-stage in-order RV32I pipeline

Modules with holes: core/ALU.v, core/CtrlUnit.v, core/HazardDetectionUnit.v, core/ImmGen.v,
core/RAM_B.v, core/Regs.v, core/REG_IF_ID.v, core/REG_ID_EX.v, core/REG_EX_MEM.v,
core/REG_MEM_WB.v, core/RV32core.v, common/cmp_32.v.

The intended microarchitecture (derived from the skeleton wiring — follow it exactly):

* Branches and jumps are resolved in the ID stage: cmp_32 lives in ID, the branch target
  adder add_branch_ID computes (JALR ? rs1_data_ID : PC_ID) + Imm_out_ID, and CtrlUnit's
  \`Branch\` output means "take the jump" (unconditional JAL/JALR, or a conditional branch
  whose cmp_res input is 1).
* mux_IF selects PC_4_IF vs jump_PC_ID using Branch_ctrl, driving next_PC_IF.
* Forwarding is done in the ID stage with MUX4T1_32 mux_forward_A / mux_forward_B:
  input 0 = register-file output (rs1_data_reg / rs2_data_reg), input 1 = the MEM-stage
  result. Create the extra wire requested by the TODO:
      wire [31:0] mem_fwd_data = DatatoReg_MEM ? Datain_MEM : ALUout_MEM;
  (loads forward the RAM output, everything else forwards the ALU output; RAM_B reads
  combinationally so the load value is available while the load is in MEM).
  Wire mux outputs to rs1_data_ID / rs2_data_ID and the select to forward_ctrl_A/B.
  Leave inputs 2 and 3 tied to something harmless (e.g. 32'b0).
* The register file is write-through, so a WB-stage producer needs no forwarding path.
* An EX-stage producer CANNOT be forwarded to ID (its result does not exist yet) → stall
  one cycle. HazardDetectionUnit therefore needs the EX-stage "does it write a register"
  information: register \`hazard_optype_ID\` once inside HazardDetectionUnit to obtain the
  EX-stage optype, and twice to obtain the MEM-stage optype (2'b10 = load, 2'b01 = other
  register write, 2'b00 = no register write).
  - stall = (optype_EX != 2'b00) && rd_EXE != 0 &&
            ((rs1use_ID && rs1_ID == rd_EXE) || (rs2use_ID && rs2_ID == rd_EXE))
  - On stall: PC_EN_IF = 0, reg_FD_EN = 1, reg_FD_stall = 1, reg_DE_EN = 1, reg_DE_flush = 1
    (bubble injected into EX). reg_EM_EN = reg_MW_EN = 1, reg_EM_flush = 0 always.
  - reg_FD_flush = Branch_ID (kill the sequentially-fetched instruction after a taken
    branch/jump). REG_IF_ID gives Data_stall priority over flush, so a stalled branch does
    not lose the delay-slot instruction.
  - forward_ctrl_A = (optype_MEM != 2'b00 && rd_MEM != 0 && rs1use_ID && rs1_ID == rd_MEM)
                     ? 2'b01 : 2'b00 ; same for B with rs2.
    Using rd_MEM alone is NOT safe: REG_ID_EX latches rd unconditionally, so a store or a
    branch carries a bogus rd — that is exactly why the optype pipeline is needed.
  - forward_ctrl_ls = (optype_MEM != 2'b00 && rd_MEM != 0 && rd_MEM == rs2_EXE); it drives
    mux_forward_EXE which selects the store data (I0 = rs2_data_EXE, I1 = mem_fwd_data,
    output = Dataout_EXE).
* mux_A_EXE: I0 = rs1_data_EXE, I1 = PC_EXE, s = ALUSrc_A_EXE, o = ALUA_EXE.
  mux_B_EXE: I0 = rs2_data_EXE, I1 = Imm_EXE,  s = ALUSrc_B_EXE, o = ALUB_EXE.
* CtrlUnit: ALUSrc_A = AUIPC | JAL | JALR (use PC), ALUSrc_B = I_valid | L_valid | S_valid |
  LUI | AUIPC | JAL | JALR (use immediate). JAL/JALR compute rd = PC+4 with ALU_Ap4 (A=PC),
  LUI passes the immediate through with ALU_Bout, AUIPC adds PC+imm.
  rs1use = R/I/S/L/B types and JALR. rs2use = R/S/B types.
  hazard_optype = 2'b10 for loads, 2'b01 for every other register-writing instruction
  (R, I, LUI, AUIPC, JAL, JALR), 2'b00 otherwise.
  cmp_ctrl must map BEQ/BNE/BLT/BLTU/BGE/BGEU onto cmp_32's cmp_EQ/NE/LT/LTU/GE/GEU codes.
  Decode all 37 RV32I instructions (fence/ecall/ebreak excluded).
* ALU: ADD SUB AND OR XOR SLL SRL SRA SLT SLTU, ALU_Ap4 (A+4), ALU_Bout (pass B).
  Shifts use only the low 5 bits of B. SLT is signed, SLTU unsigned. zero = (res == 0).
  overflow = signed overflow of ADD/SUB only.
* ImmGen: standard RV32I I/B/J/S/U immediates (B and J immediates already include the <<1).
* RAM_B: 128 bytes, little endian, data[0:127]; write only when wea and addra[31:7]==0;
  mem_u_b_h_w[1]=word, [0]=half, else byte; [2]=zero-extend else sign-extend on read;
  reads are combinational and return 0 when out of range.
* Regs: 31 x 32-bit (register[1:31]), x0 hardwired 0, synchronous reset, write on the
  clock edge when L_S is asserted, combinational read with write-through, Debug_regs port.

Verification: /workspace/repo/src/lab1/all_test.s documents, for nearly every instruction,
its PC and the register value it must produce; core/rom.mem is exactly that program.
Write a testbench that instantiates RV32core (like sim/core_sim.v), and on every rising edge
records (PC_WB, inst_WB, rd_WB, wt_data_WB) whenever RegWrite_WB is set, then compares that
trace against the expectations from all_test.s. EVERY documented value must match, including
the branch/jump section at the end of the file, and the memory (sb/sh/sw + lb/lh/lbu/lhu)
section. Also make sure the program's final jump/loop behaviour is right.
Read all_test.s completely and encode all of its expectations.
`,
  },
  {
    id: 'lab2',
    title: 'Lab 2 — CSR + exceptions',
    prompt: `
# Your lab: src/lab2 — 5-stage pipeline + M-mode CSRs + exception unit

Modules with holes: core/ALU.v, core/CtrlUnit.v, core/CSRRegs.v, core/ExceptionUnit.v,
core/HazardDetectionUnit.v, core/ImmGen.v, core/RAM_B.v, core/Regs.v, core/REG_IF_ID.v,
core/REG_ID_EX.v, core/REG_EX_MEM.v, core/REG_MEM_WB.v, core/RV32core.v.

src/lab1 is the same base pipeline (ID-stage branch resolution + ID-stage forwarding, MEM->ID
forwarding only, one stall cycle for an EX-stage producer). Read src/lab1 first — but note
lab1 is ALSO being implemented right now by another agent, so lab1's files may be empty or
mid-edit: rely on lab2's own skeleton comments, port lists and docs/lab2.md, and on lab3 /
lab4 for cross-reference. Never edit lab1.

Additional lab2 semantics you must get right (read docs/lab2.md and core/*.v carefully):
* CSRRegs: CSR file addressed by the 12-bit CSR address; supports CSRRW / CSRRS / CSRRC
  (and their immediate forms). Reads return the old value; writes happen on the clock edge.
  It also holds the machine-mode CSRs used by the exception unit (mstatus 0x300, mtvec 0x305,
  mepc 0x341, mcause 0x342, mtval 0x343, mip 0x344 ...). Follow the port list and the
  comments in the file exactly.
* ExceptionUnit: detects illegal instruction, ecall, load/store access fault and the external
  interrupt, writes mepc/mcause/mtval/mstatus, redirects the PC to mtvec (and back to mepc on
  MRET) and produces the flush / cancel signals that suppress the register write and the
  memory write of the faulting instruction and of everything younger.
* RV32core: add the exception redirect mux on next_PC and the cancel signals.

Verification: /workspace/repo/src/lab2/exp_test.s is the program in core/rom.mem and its
comments give the expected register values, the expected CSR values, and the expected
mepc/mcause/mtval for each of the four traps. Build a testbench under
/workspace/agent_tests/lab2/ that traces the WB stage (PC_WB / inst_WB / rd_WB / wt_data_WB /
RegWrite_WB) plus the CSR file contents, and check the documented expectations:
csrrwi/csrr/csrrw sequences, mtvec setup, then the traps
(1) ecall at 0x38 -> mcause 0x0000000b, mepc 0x38, mtval 0
(2) illegal instruction -> mcause 2, mtval = the instruction word
(3) load access fault -> mcause 5, mtval = the faulting address 0x80
(4) store access fault -> mcause 7, mtval = 0x80
and mstatus 0x00001880 as documented in exp_test.s.
Report honestly which of these you verified.
`,
  },
  {
    id: 'lab3',
    title: 'Lab 3 — pipeline with UART-simulating RAM',
    prompt: `
# Your lab: src/lab3 — standalone 5-stage RV32I pipeline with simulated UART output

Modules with holes: core/ALU.v, core/CtrlUnit.v, core/HazardDetectionUnit.v, core/ImmGen.v,
core/RAM_B.v, core/Regs.v, core/REG_IF_ID.v, core/REG_ID_EX.v, core/REG_EX_MEM.v,
core/REG_MEM_WB.v, core/RV32core.v, common/cmp_32.v.

This is the same family of design as src/lab1 (read lab1's skeleton for the shape, but lab3
has its own, slightly larger control signal set — CtrlUnit also emits CSR read/write control
signals and a 2-bit exception vector, and HazardDetectionUnit handles the wider signal set).
Follow lab3's OWN port lists and comments; do not blindly copy lab1. Note lab1/lab2 are being
implemented concurrently by other agents, so their files may be incomplete — never edit them.

Special: RAM_B implements a simulated UART. A word store to address 0x10000000 must print the
ASCII character in the low byte (use $write("%c", ...) so the simulation prints the program's
output). Normal data memory occupies the low address range as documented in the file.

The program in core/rom.mem is a sort benchmark; sources and a full disassembly are in
lab3_ref/src/sort.c and lab3_ref/obj/sort-riscv32-cpu.txt. Read the disassembly to know the
memory map, the entry point and what output the program prints.

Verification: build /workspace/agent_tests/lab3/ that runs the CPU for enough cycles and
captures the UART output; the program must run to completion and print the sorted result
exactly as sort.c implies. Also add sanity checks on the WB trace (PC_WB / rd_WB /
wt_data_WB / RegWrite_WB) for the first dozen instructions. Report the captured UART text.
`,
  },
  {
    id: 'lab4',
    title: 'Lab 4 — pipeline variant + cache hierarchy',
    prompt: `
# Your lab: src/lab4 — 5-stage pipeline whose MEM stage talks to a CMU + cache + data_ram

Holes: core/ALU.v, core/CtrlUnit.v, core/HazardDetectionUnit.v, core/ImmGen.v, core/Regs.v,
core/REG_IF_ID.v, core/REG_ID_EX.v, core/REG_EX_MEM.v, core/REG_MEM_WB.v, core/RV32core.v,
AND cache/cache.v which still contains 19 \`//need to fill in\` course-skeleton blanks (the
file currently does not even compile). cache/cmu.v, cache/data_ram.v and cache/addr_define.vh
are provided — read them to learn the exact protocol the cache must implement.

cache.v is a 2-way set-associative, write-back, LRU cache: 64 elements / 2 ways = 32 sets,
ELEMENT_WORDS words per line. Every blank is the "way 2" mirror of an existing "way 1"
expression (addr_element2 = {addr_index, 1'b1}, word2 = inner_data[addr_word2], hit2 =
valid2 & (tag2 == addr_tag), etc.), plus the registered outputs (valid/dirty/tag/hit must be
registered from the way selected by the LRU \`recent1\` bit exactly the way the surrounding
code and cmu.v expect) and the hit2 branches of the load / edit / store / invalid logic which
mirror the hit1 branches. Derive each blank from its way-1 twin and from how cmu.v drives and
samples the cache.

The pipeline uses a DIFFERENT control-signal encoding than lab1 (e.g. 2-bit DatatoReg /
PCSource style signals) — follow lab4's own port lists and comments. HazardDetectionUnit must
additionally propagate the CMU's \`cmu_stall\` signal so the whole pipeline freezes on a cache
miss (PC and all pipeline latches disabled, no spurious re-execution of the memory access).

Verification: src/lab4/mem_test.s (assembled into core/rom.mem) documents each access and
whether it hits or misses, and cache/ram.mem holds the backing data. Build
/workspace/agent_tests/lab4/ that runs the core and checks:
  - the register values produced by the load sequence (lb/lh/lw/lbu/lhu of 0xF0F0F0F0 at 0x1C
    give 0xFFFFFFF0 / 0xFFFFF0F0 / 0xF0F0F0F0 / 0x000000F0 / 0x0000F0F0),
  - the hit/miss sequence matches the comments in mem_test.s,
  - the dirty-line write-back actually reaches data_ram,
  - the program reaches the final loop with x16 = 0xED.
Also compile-check cache/cmu.v with sim/cmu_sim.v if that helps. Report the trace.
`,
  },
  {
    id: 'lab5',
    title: 'Lab 5 — scoreboard out-of-order',
    prompt: `
# Your lab: src/lab5 — scoreboard-based out-of-order RV32IM core

TWO groups of holes:
(a) The five functional units core/FU_ALU.v, FU_mul.v, FU_div.v, FU_jump.v, FU_mem.v
    (marked with TODO).
(b) core/CtrlUnit.v — the scoreboard itself — still contains 64 \`//fill sth. here\`
    course-skeleton blanks with literal \`...\` tokens. THE FILE DOES NOT COMPILE TODAY.
    You must complete all of them. This is the heart of the lab.

Read core/CtrlDefine.vh (field offsets of the FUS table and the op encodings), core/RV32core.v
(already complete — it shows exactly how the CtrlUnit outputs are consumed), core/Regs.v,
core/REG_IF_IS.v and docs/lab5.md (contains the formal scoreboard algorithm).

Scoreboard structure already declared in CtrlUnit.v:
  reg[31:0] FUS[1:5];   // per-FU status: BUSY, OP, DST, SRC1, SRC2, FU1(Qj), FU2(Qk),
                        // RDY1(Rj), RDY2(Rk), FU_DONE  — bit positions in CtrlDefine.vh
  reg[2:0]  RRS[0:31];  // register result status: which FU will write each register
  reg[31:0] IMM[1:5], PCR[1:5];
What each blank needs:
* normal_stall — issue must stall on a structural hazard (the target FU is already BUSY, or
  is finishing/occupied) or on WAW (RRS[dst] != 0 for a writing instruction). Also account
  for jump_stall (an in-flight jump blocks issue) as the skeleton intends.
* The IS block: on RO_en, fill FUS[use_FU] with BUSY/op/dst/src1/src2/fu1/fu2/rdy1/rdy2 and
  set RRS[dst].
* The RO blocks: for each FU, when both operands are ready, clear RDY1/RDY2 and the Qj/Qk
  fields (operands have been read). Keep the same priority order as the combinational
  RO always block further down the file (JUMP, ALU, MEM, MUL, DIV) — the two must agree
  exactly, otherwise the enables and the table updates diverge.
* The EX block: FUS[x][FU_DONE] <= the corresponding *_done input (latching completion).
* The WB blocks: when FU_DONE & the FU's WAR guard, clear FUS[x] and RRS[dst], and wake up
  every other FU that was waiting on this FU (if FUS[y][FU1]==x then set RDY1 and clear FU1;
  same for FU2) — that is the RAW resolution. Only ONE register write per cycle is possible,
  so the WB priority order must match the combinational WB always block at the end of the
  file (JUMP, ALU, MEM, MUL, DIV).
* The *_WAR guards: FU x may write its destination only if no other FU still has an unread
  source operand equal to x's destination. Each line has the shape
      (FUS[other][SRCn] != FUS[x][DST] | ~FUS[other][RDYn])
  — i.e. either the register differs, or that operand has already been read.
  Work out the exact polarity from the RDY semantics used in the RO blocks (RDY=1 means
  "operand not yet read but available"; it is cleared when the operand is read).

Functional units: each is a small state machine, all documented in their TODO comments.
* FU_ALU: 1-cycle. Latch ALUA/ALUB/ALUControl on (EN & ~state), state<=1, finish = state.
  Full ALU (same op encoding as ALU.v in lab1: ADD 0001, SUB 0010, AND 0011, OR 0100,
  XOR 0101, SLL 0110, SRL 0111, SLT 1000, SLTU 1001, SRA 1010, A+4 1011, B-passthrough 1100).
* FU_mul: latch on (EN & ~|state), state <= 7'b100_0000 then shift right each cycle,
  finish = state[0]. Result = low 32 bits of A*B. Do NOT instantiate the missing Vivado
  \`multiplier\` IP — write your own helper module with a unique name inside FU_mul.v whose
  latency fits inside the state-machine window, or compute it directly.
* FU_div: the skeleton declares \`wire res_valid; wire[63:0] divres;\` and
  \`assign finish = res_valid & state;\`. Implement your own uniquely-named divider helper
  module inside FU_div.v with an AXI-ish valid handshake: it accepts A (dividend) and B
  (divisor) when A_valid/B_valid are high and asserts res_valid some cycles later with
  divres = {quotient, remainder}; res = divres[63:32]. Choose the latency so the reference
  timing in ref/inst.S is reproduced as closely as possible (see below) — around 36 cycles
  from acceptance to res_valid is what the Vivado Divider Generator gives.
* FU_jump: 1 cycle; cmp_32 on the latched rs1/rs2 with the latched cmp_ctrl;
  PC_jump = (JALR ? rs1 : PC) + imm; PC_wb = PC + 4; is_jump = cmp_ctrl[0] | cmp_res.
  (careful: FU_jump's cmp_ctrl port is 4 bits = Jump_ctrl[3:0]; bit 0 of the JUMP op encoding
  marks an unconditional jump, and bits [3:1] are the cmp_32 ctrl — see CtrlDefine.vh
  JUMP_* encodings and cmp_32's parameter values.)
* FU_mem: latch on (EN & ~|state), state <= 2'b10 then shift right, finish = state[0];
  address = rs1_data + imm via add_32; instantiate the provided RAM_B.

Verification: ref/inst.S is the program in core/rom.mem, annotated with the value each
instruction writes AND the value of clk_counter when that write becomes visible. Build
/workspace/agent_tests/lab5/ with a testbench that instantiates RV32core (ports: debug_en,
debug_step, debug_addr, debug_data, wb_addr, wb_data, clk_counter, clk, rst, interrupter),
traces every (clk_counter, wb_addr, wb_data) write and compares against ref/inst.S. All the
register VALUES must match and the write ORDER must be out-of-order exactly as annotated
(e.g. \`mul x9,x4,x5\` retires before \`div x8,x7,x2\`). Getting the clk_counter values close
to the annotations is a strong signal you got the scoreboard right; report both.
`,
  },
  {
    id: 'lab6',
    title: 'Lab 6 — Tomasulo out-of-order',
    prompt: `
# Your lab: src/lab6 — Tomasulo out-of-order RV32IM core with reservation stations and a CDB

Holes: core/FU_ALU.v, FU_mul.v, FU_div.v, FU_jump.v, FU_mem.v (identical to lab5's FUs),
core/CtrlUnit.v, core/Regs.v (register file + RAT), core/RAM_B.v, core/ImmGen.v, and
core/RV32core.v (22 TODOs — the whole Tomasulo top level).

IMPORTANT: RV32core.v instantiates a module named \`RS\` which DOES NOT EXIST anywhere in this
repo. You must NOT define a module called \`RS\` (the grading harness may supply its own).
Instead define your own reservation-station module with a unique name (e.g.
\`rs_station_lab6\`) at the bottom of RV32core.v and change the instantiations to use it.
You are free to give it whatever ports you need, but you MUST keep the surrounding
RV32core.v signal names (cdb_rs_num, cdb_data, cdb_pc, rs_num_rd, rs_num_A, rs_num_B,
ALU_src1, ALU_src2, ALU_op, ALU_pc, FU_*_EN, FU_*_finish, wb_addr, wb_data, clk_counter, ...)
because the hidden tests reference them hierarchically, and you must keep
\`assign wb_addr = cdb_pc; assign wb_data = cdb_data;\` semantics: wb_addr carries the PC of
the instruction whose result is on the CDB and wb_data carries that result.
Likewise never instantiate the missing \`multiplier\` / \`divider\` IPs — implement your own
uniquely-named helper modules inside FU_mul.v / FU_div.v exactly as described for lab5.

Design requirements:
* Regs.v: a register file with an integrated RAT. Ports already present include rs_rd_w_en,
  R_addr_rd, rs_num_rd, rs_num_A, rs_num_B, cdb_rs_num, cdb_data, R_addr_A/B, rdata_A/B,
  Debug_addr/Debug_regs. rs_num_A/rs_num_B output the 8-bit RS tag currently owning
  R_addr_A / R_addr_B (0 = value is in the register file). On issue (rs_rd_w_en) RAT[rd] is
  set to the allocated RS tag. On a CDB broadcast, every register whose RAT entry equals
  cdb_rs_num gets cdb_data written and its RAT entry cleared. x0 always reads 0 and is never
  renamed.
* CtrlUnit.v: pure decode — ImmSel, rs1_ctrl, rs2_ctrl, dst_ctrl, ALU_use_PC, ALU_use_imm,
